opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, I've been doing security and networking research for a long time, and for most of my career the threat model was pretty familiar: attackers trying to break into systems, steal data, disrupt services. What shifted for me over the last several years is realizing that some of the most consequential harms weren't coming from a classic attacker at all. They were coming from very powerful AI systems being deployed at scale, often by well-resourced companies, in ways that the people affected had no say in and no real way to push back against.

Early on, a lot of our work was around things like facial recognition. We saw images scraped from people's social media and used to build recognition models without anyone's knowledge or consent. That felt like a clear case where the individual had essentially zero leverage. You can't opt out of something you don't know is happening, and the law was way behind. So we started asking a security researcher's question: if the system is going to consume your data whether you like it or not, can we change the data itself so that what it learns is wrong, or at least not useful against you? That line of thinking led to tools that perturb images in ways that are hard for people to see but meaningfully disrupt what a model learns.

Then generative AI came along, and the problem got much bigger and much more personal. We started hearing from artists, illustrators, and other creatives who were watching models trained on their life's work produce imitations of their style on demand, sometimes under their name. For many of them it wasn't abstract. It was their income, their identity, years of practice, and they felt completely powerless. Hearing those stories directly was a big turning point for me. It made it clear that this wasn't just an interesting technical puzzle, it was a question of who holds power when these systems are built.

So what really draws me to this area is that asymmetry. Security research, at its best, is about protecting people who are vulnerable against those with more capability. Right now, in a lot of AI deployments, individuals are on the losing side of a huge imbalance. If we can build tools that give some agency back, even partially, even imperfectly, while policy and norms catch up, that feels like one of the most meaningful uses of what we know how to do as security researchers.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from traditional security and networking threats toward protecting people harmed by AI deployments. It does not say Zhao’s earlier research focused on defending machine learning systems, so the full stated shift is not communicated.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, I've been a security person for most of my career, and the way I think about security is really about who's getting hurt and who has power. When machine learning started taking off, I noticed something: a lot of the conversation was about how to make these systems better, more accurate, more capable. Very little of it was about the people on the receiving end, the ones who had no say in how these models were built or deployed.

A lot of it started with facial recognition. Companies like Clearview were scraping billions of photos off the internet, building models that could identify anyone, and the people in those photos never consented to any of it. That felt like a classic security problem to me, just with a different attacker. The victim isn't a corporation with a server to patch. It's an individual who posted a picture of their kid at a birthday party. So we built Fawkes, which lets you cloak your photos so they poison the models trained on them, and that was really the first time we thought, okay, maybe we can actually give normal people a tool to push back.

Then generative AI happened, and the same pattern showed up again, only bigger. Artists suddenly found that their entire life's work had been ingested into models that could mimic their style in seconds, and they were being told there was nothing they could do about it. We got hundreds of emails from artists, some of them really heartbreaking. People losing commissions, people questioning whether they should keep making art at all. That's where Glaze and later Nightshade came from.

So I guess what draws me is the asymmetry. You have a handful of very well-resourced companies on one side and individuals with basically no leverage on the other. Security research, at its best, is about restoring some balance. I don't think technical tools solve the whole problem, you need regulation and policy too, but they buy people time and give them a way to say no that actually means something. That's what keeps me motivated.

r001.rationale: He contrasts the field’s focus on making machine learning systems better with his concern for people affected by their deployment, describing his work as protecting individuals from AI misuse.

astra-6.text:
For me, security has always been about people. We can get very focused on the technical problem—how a system fails, how an attacker gets in—but the reason those problems matter is that somebody gets hurt.

With AI, I’m interested in that gap between what a technology makes possible and what people can do to protect themselves when it’s used against them. If you’re on the receiving end of misuse, you may have very little control over the system and very little ability to challenge the people deploying it.

That’s a compelling research problem to me: can we give those people some agency? Can we build something that lets them protect themselves? The technical work is interesting, but helping people is what gives it purpose.

r001.rationale: The response describes protecting people from AI misuse, but it does not say Ben Zhao’s research focus shifted from defending machine learning systems to protecting people.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, security research starts with people. We often talk about whether a system is secure in a technical sense, but the more fundamental question is: who gets hurt when it fails, or when someone uses it in a way it wasn’t intended to be used?

AI makes that question particularly pressing because it can give a relatively small number of people the ability to affect a very large number of others. And the people affected don’t necessarily have a say in how these systems are built or deployed.

That’s what draws me to this work: asking what we can do, as researchers, to give people some agency. Can we build tools that let them protect themselves, rather than making their protection depend entirely on the goodwill of whoever controls the technology? Those are challenging technical problems, but they also have a very concrete human purpose.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes protecting people from AI misuse, but it does not describe a shift from previously defending machine learning systems.
